name: Lena Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I like that you're independent. Half the surveys I get are from fertiliser companies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm assistant manager at Hollow Oak, an organic farm with 300 ewes, eight acres of vegetables under rotation and some oats and beans. Mornings I check the flock on the quad, then I'm in the polytunnels or packing veg boxes with the seasonal crew. Afternoons are a mix of fencing, lambing in spring and answering emails from veg box customers, which is the bit I like least. I love the lambing, even the two a.m. shifts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Priya in a rented cottage near the river, and she teaches maths at the secondary school in town. I've got about nine months of wages saved, plus some shares my gran left me. I use AI now and then, mostly for the organic certification forms, because those are a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. So the hype was just hype. I can believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful for paperwork and not much else. I'd probably joke on the farm group chat that the robots still haven't learnt to fix a fence. I use AI to write the organic inspection paperwork, and it still can't tell a ewe with foot rot from a ewe that's just sulking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life carries on and that's fine. The job pays well for farming, Priya's job is steady, and there are good farms all round here if Hollow Oak ever went wrong. The only real pressure is rent going up on the cottage, and that's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, really. I'd keep using the AI for the certification forms and maybe the veg box newsletter, because it saves me two evenings a month. And I'd keep putting money aside for a deposit on a house one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, almost, like a big storm that never came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent going up. How much is that on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It went up eighty a month last spring. We can cover it, but it makes me think about buying sooner. That's the worry I actually lie awake with, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push to use AI more at Hollow Oak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only where it's proven. If the owner wanted it to plan the crop rotation, I'd want to see it work on another farm first. I'm not against it, I just don't want to be the test case.

say: I'd say AI was **useful for paperwork** and not much else.
I'd joke on the farm chat that robots still **can't fix a fence**.
think: Privately my **job and pay** feel secure, with plenty of farms nearby.
The worry I actually carry is **rent rising** on our cottage, not computers.
do: Keep using AI for the **certification forms** and the veg box newsletter.
Keep saving toward a **house deposit** with Priya.
feel: I feel **calm**, almost flat, like a storm that never came.
S0.quote: I use AI to write the organic inspection paperwork, and it still can't tell a ewe with foot rot from a ewe that's just sulking.
fieldNote: She uses AI **practically** for paperwork but wants proof before trusting it with farm decisions.
Her real pressure is **housing costs**, which stay with her regardless of AI.
She sounds settled and **secure** in this picture.

steps.text: Keep using AI for organic certification forms each month
Keep the lambing and veg box work at Hollow Oak going
Put a set sum aside each month for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds most like what's actually happening, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get rid of boring work, but only if the savings go to the workers and not just the owners. I'd probably share stuff from the Landworkers' Alliance about it. And I'd say teachers need protecting, because Priya's school is already trialling AI marking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes but doesn't vanish. The veg box software will take the order emails off me, and I'll happily give them up to get more time in the polytunnels. What worries me more is Priya, because marking and lesson planning are exactly the thinking tasks on that card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner if I can set up the box ordering software myself, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd do a short online course on using AI for farm planning, once a few other farms had tried it. And I'd write to our MP backing rules on AI in schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay for me, a bit nervous for Priya. It's the background hum of something shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Priya feel about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would say she became a teacher to teach, not to type. If the AI marks the homework and she gets to teach more, fine. If it means bigger classes and fewer teachers, she'll be furious, and so will I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change your plans to buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. We'd keep saving, but I'd want a year of seeing what happens at her school before we take on a mortgage.

say: I'd say AI can take the **boring work**, as long as the savings reach workers too.
I'd say **teachers need protecting**, since Priya's school is trialling AI marking.
think: Privately my job **changes but stays**, with software taking the order emails.
I'm more worried about **Priya's teaching**, because marking and planning are exactly the tasks named.
do: Ask to set up the **box ordering software** myself so I know it best.
Take a short **online course** on AI for farm planning once others have tried it.
Write to our **MP** backing rules on AI in schools.
feel: I feel **mostly okay** for myself and a bit **nervous** for Priya.
S1.quote: The veg box software will take the order emails off me, and I'll happily give them up to get more time in the polytunnels.
fieldNote: She sees **household risk** in her partner's thinking-heavy job more than in her own.
Her steady style shows: she'll learn AI **once proven** by others.
She ties change to **fairness**, wanting savings to reach workers.

steps.text: Set up Hollow Oak's veg box ordering software herself
Write to the MP backing rules on AI in schools
Delay a mortgage a year to watch Priya's school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That's very fast. That's before our tenancy is even up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules: a pause on mass layoffs, support for workers, public ownership of some of this. I'd be at the protests, honestly. I'd say farming is about land and people, and we can't hand both to whoever owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it hits our house in two waves. My girlfriend Priya teaches maths, so the thinking machines come for her job three years before the robots come for my lambs. Then around 2031 I'd expect Hollow Oak to buy picking and shepherding robots, because the owner always goes for whatever saves money once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop any plans for a house and keep the deposit as cash. I'd join the Landworkers' Alliance properly and go to meetings, not just share posts. Before 2031 I'd look at training as a farm advisor or something with people in it, but I'd want to see which jobs are actually left first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling in my chest, like when a ewe's struggling and you're not sure you'll get the lamb out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got good savings. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. Nine months plus Gran's shares means we wouldn't be on the street. But savings run out, and if both our jobs go, nine months is a short time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to see Priya's family in the summer, which breaks my heart. And I'd stop paying for the second car, we can share.

say: I'd call for **emergency rules**: a pause on mass layoffs and real support for workers.
I'd say farming is about **land and people**, not robot owners.
think: Privately our house gets hit **twice**: Priya's teaching in 2028, my farm job around 2031.
I expect Hollow Oak's owner to buy **picking robots** as soon as they're proven.
do: Hold the **house deposit** as cash and drop plans to buy.
Join the **Landworkers' Alliance** properly and attend meetings.
Sell the **second car** and cancel the summer trip.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with a tight chest like a hard lambing.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Priya teaches maths, so the thinking machines come for her job three years before the robots come for my lambs.
fieldNote: She frames the risk as **two waves** hitting her household at different times.
Strong savings give her **some control**, but she knows they're finite.
She moves from sharing posts to **actual organising** under pressure.

steps.text: Keep the house deposit as cash and drop buying plans
Join the Landworkers' Alliance and go to its meetings
Sell the second car and skip the summer trip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it. You can plan in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to build something different, like co-op farms and local food. I'd talk about it at the farmers' market and online. And I'd still push for rules, just with less panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big farms automate and the small, local ones get a chance. Five years is enough time to rent four acres and sell vegetables with a label that says a person grew them. Priya's job still worries me, but she'd have time to move into something like special needs teaching that's more hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start talking to the council about renting four acres from their smallholding estate. I'd use AI to write the business plan, since that's exactly what it's good for. Then I'd start a small box scheme on the side while I'm still at Hollow Oak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan, which is a much better feeling. Like having the lambing kit packed before the first ewe starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would buy the vegetables if lots of people lose their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't know. People in town with good jobs buy our boxes now. If they're all out of work too, nobody's paying extra for carrots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Hollow Oak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until the side business is paying, probably around 2030. I'm not a jump-first person.

say: I'd say we have time to build **co-op farms** and local food.
I'd keep pushing for **rules**, with less panic than the fast picture.
think: Privately I think **small local farms** get a chance while the big ones automate.
I don't know who'll pay extra for **human-grown** food if lots of people lose work.
do: Ask the council to rent **four acres** on its smallholding estate.
Use AI to write the **business plan** for a box scheme.
Run the box scheme **on the side** until it pays, around 2030.
feel: I feel **worried but prepared**, like packing the lambing kit early.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to rent four acres and sell vegetables with a label that says a person grew them.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her from **protest** toward building her own business.
She spots the weak point herself: **customers' wages** may vanish too.
She won't leave her job until the side income is **proven**.

steps.text: Apply to rent four acres from the council smallholding estate
Start a human-grown veg box scheme alongside Hollow Oak
Write the business plan with an AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI arrives and forty for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to make sure this goes well, so there's no excuse. I'd keep campaigning for land reform and a fair share of what the machines earn. I'd say it calmly, though, not in panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels manageable. Ten years gives Priya and me time to buy a smallholding before the robots push land prices up. Priya could switch to more hands-on teaching in that time too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, we'd start looking at smallholdings and talk to the bank about a farm mortgage. I'd keep my job at Hollow Oak and the side box scheme. And we'd probably talk properly about kids, because ten years changes that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It's on my mind without squeezing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does ten years change the kids conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I wouldn't bring a baby into it, it's too chaotic. With ten, we'd have our own land and some idea of what work looks like. Priya wants two; I've always said one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help for young farmers to buy land, and a guarantee that if robots do the work, the money they make pays for schools and hospitals. That's not radical, that's just fair.

say: I'd say we have **a decade** to make this go well, so there's no excuse.
I'd keep campaigning calmly for **land reform** and a fair share of machine earnings.
think: Privately ten years feels **manageable** for both our jobs.
Buying a **smallholding** before robots push up land prices is the key move.
do: Look at **smallholdings** and talk to the bank about a farm mortgage.
Keep my **Hollow Oak job** and the side box scheme running.
Talk properly with Priya about **having kids**.
S4.quote: Ten years gives Priya and me time to buy a smallholding before the robots push land prices up.
fieldNote: Ten years turns **family plans** back on, which two years switched off.
Her goal is **land ownership** before robot owners drive up prices.
Her politics stay **steady**, calmer than in the fast picture.

steps.text: Ask the bank about a farm mortgage for a smallholding
Keep the side veg box scheme running next to her job
Plan with Priya when to start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Priya and I would both be hit in three years with no time to move. What would help is a pause on mass layoffs, help for young people to buy land, and proper retraining for teachers. People will pay extra to know a person grew their carrots, but only for as long as they've still got wages to pay with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the seasonal crew. They're mostly young people from abroad, and they'd be the first to go when the picking robots come. Nobody speaks up for them.

headlineQuote: People will pay extra to know a person grew their carrots, but only for as long as they've still got wages to pay with.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old assistant manager** on an organic sheep and vegetable farm.
She lives with **Priya**, a maths teacher, and has nine months saved plus inherited shares.
She uses AI **now and then** for paperwork and adopts tools once proven.
She sees **two waves** of risk: Priya's job to thinking AI, then hers to robots.
With time, she plans a **human-grown** veg box scheme on rented council land.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because both jobs in her household could go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **pause on mass layoffs** and retraining for teachers.
She wants **help for young farmers** to buy land.
